extracted.intended_audience: peer reviewers, editors, and other participants in scientific publishing (including early-career researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for ethical conduct by reviewers and editors when evaluating manuscripts for scholarly journals, covering conflicts, confidentiality, credit, critique style, and courteous behavior. Also addresses emerging challenges such as AI and integrity screening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A fair and impartial review is possible only when it is free from any competing interests and conscious or unconscious biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reveal obvious conflicts (same institutional affiliation, prior significant collaborations) and intellectual or financial conflicts that may affect the review outcome before agreeing to review. If uncertain what constitutes a conflict, communicate it to the journal's staff. Avoid unethical requests such as suggesting authors cite the reviewer's own work to boost personal citation metrics or in expectation of future favors. Be mindful of conscious and unconscious biases (favorable or opposing views about the study, country of origin, type of institutional affiliation, gender or race of the corresponding author) and how underrepresentation (e.g., gender gaps among editors/reviewers) can affect outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors entrust journals, editors and reviewers to maintain the confidentiality of unpublished work while it is under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not disclose, discuss, share, or comment on manuscript content until it is published. Avoid misuse of unpublished material for your own research. Obtain permission from the journal before involving others (e.g., postdocs or graduate students) in the review process; journals may have specific policies for including co-reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit (recognition and transparency for reviewers and co-reviewers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should provide credit to individuals who devote time to performing reviews; transparency is needed to ensure early-career co-reviewers receive acknowledgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'ghostwriting' of reviews where mentored co-reviewers are not credited. Use mentored co-reviewing and reviewer training programs to give credit and build a pool of trained reviewers (examples: ASM Microbiology Spectrum Reviewer Editor Program, mBio Early Career Reviewer Program). Recognize reviewer contributions when appropriate, as many reviewers seek acknowledgment for their work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive Criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review should assess the science, identifying strengths and weaknesses while providing unbiased, honest critiques that help improve the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide constructive, actionable suggestions that clarify how the authors can improve their manuscript. Do not intentionally sabotage competitors by supplying unfair negative comments, requesting unjustified experiments, or making demands meant to harm outcomes. For manuscripts with major weaknesses, clearly explain the issues and suggest concrete remedies to reach publishable quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtesy
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must deliver a fair, honest and unbiased assessment while maintaining professional tone and civility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ad hominem or unprofessional comments; editors may edit out such language. Be thorough and consistent to support editorial decision-making. Respectfully note if the manuscript would benefit from improvements in flow, grammar, or clarity and, where helpful, point authors to copy-editing or language-editing services. Courteous behavior supports trust in the review process and enables diversity, equity, and inclusion to be heard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of AI and automated tools in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: The evolving role of artificial intelligence and digital tools presents ethical challenges for peer review and scholarly publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that AI tools may assist screening or pre-review tasks but cannot replace human judgement for complex assessments (e.g., whether experiments properly test hypotheses or the implications of a study). Be cautious about over-reliance on automated tools and consider ethical implications of using AI to assess manuscripts; human reviewers and editors should remain responsible for substantive evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher integrity screening (plagiarism and image manipulation detection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers increasingly use automated systems to detect plagiarism and potential image manipulation as part of pre-publication screening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that journals may pre-screen submissions (e.g., CrossCheck for textual overlap and tools for image manipulation) to safeguard against misconduct. Such proactive measures are part of maintaining high-quality, trustworthy publications; reviewers should cooperate with integrity checks and alert editors to suspected misconduct.
